set_title: Polyuria, thirst and a sodium problem
stem: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia passes large volumes of urine. Serum sodium is 130 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 70 mOsm/kg. After a supervised night without water, urine osmolality is 620 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 26M + schizophrenia + polyuria + Na 130 + urine osm 70 → 620 after a night without water → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Central DI keeps the urine **dilute when water is withheld**; his reached 620 mOsm/kg
whyNot.C: Nephrogenic DI also keeps the urine **dilute without water**, and gives a high sodium, not 130
whyNot.D: SIADH makes the urine **concentrated at baseline**; his was 70 mOsm/kg
whyNot.E: Osmotic diuresis needs **glucose in the urine**; nothing here suggests it, and urine of 70 is far too dilute

why: Drinking too much lowers the sodium and suppresses ADH, so the urine is dilute. **Once water is withheld, ADH rises and the urine concentrates normally**, which proves both the pituitary and the kidney work.

head: Serum sodium
Urine at baseline
Water deprivation, then desmopressin
Typical setting
rows: **Stays dilute without water, then rises by more than 50% after desmopressin**
**Stays dilute even after desmopressin** (ADH already high)
**Concentrates when water is withheld**; little further rise with desmopressin
**Inappropriately concentrated (above 100 mOsm/kg) with urine sodium above 40 mEq/L**
Small cell lung cancer, CNS disease, drugs; euvolemic
**Glucose in the urine**; osmolality near plasma, not very dilute

idea.rule: Low sodium + dilute urine that concentrates without water = the patient is drinking too much.
also: Long-standing polydipsia washes out the medullary gradient, so the rise can be blunted

set_title: Low blood glucose with sweating or confusion: whose insulin, or no insulin at all
stem: A 27-year-old woman who does not have diabetes has recurrent episodes of sweating and confusion. During an episode, glucose is 32 mg/dL and serum insulin is high. A sulfonylurea screen is negative. C-peptide is low.
oneliner: 27F + no diabetes + recurrent sweating and confusion + glucose 32 mg/dL + high insulin + negative screen + low C-peptide → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Sulfonylureas raise C-peptide and the screen is positive; hers is **low** and the screen is **negative**
whyNot.C: Von Gierke disease has low insulin; hers is **high**
whyNot.D: Insulin excess from treatment needs known diabetes; she **does not have diabetes**
whyNot.E: Insulinoma makes insulin with C-peptide, so C-peptide is high; hers is **low**

why: Injected insulin raises the insulin level, while the pancreas senses the low glucose and shuts off its own secretion, so C-peptide and proinsulin are low. **High insulin with a low C-peptide and a negative screen** in a patient without diabetes means self-injected insulin.

head: Insulin
C-peptide and proinsulin
Sulfonylurea screen
Lactate, liver and setting
rows: Fasting hypoglycemia relieved by glucose; beta-cell tumor of the pancreas
No diabetes; access to insulin, as in a health care worker
**Known diabetes on insulin** with an extra dose, a missed meal or exercise
**Lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia and a large liver** since infancy

idea.rule: High insulin with a low C-peptide means the insulin came from outside.
also: C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin
Commercial insulin assays may not detect some analogs
Factitious disorder is more common in health care workers

set_title: Low blood glucose with sweating or confusion: whose insulin, or no insulin at all
stem: A 6-year-old girl has recurrent hypoglycemia that resolves with intravenous dextrose. Insulin given by a caregiver and von Gierke disease are both being considered.
oneliner: 6F + recurrent hypoglycemia + resolves with dextrose → Insulin given by a caregiver or von Gierke disease?
ask: Which single finding favours insulin given by a caregiver over von Gierke disease?

options.A: Glucose below 40 mg/dL during an episode
options.D: High serum insulin with a low C-peptide
options.E: Episodes that keep recurring over several months

whyNot.A: Both drop glucose low enough to cause symptoms, so the value does not separate them
whyNot.B: Dextrose corrects the low glucose in **both**
whyNot.C: Adrenergic symptoms follow low glucose from **any** cause

answer: High serum insulin with a low C-peptide
why: Both cause recurrent hypoglycemia that dextrose reverses. In von Gierke disease insulin is appropriately low, whereas injected insulin gives **high insulin with a low C-peptide**; this pattern in a child should prompt a report for factitious disorder imposed on another.

C-peptide and proinsulin
Sulfonylurea screen
Lactate, liver and setting
rows: Fasting hypoglycemia relieved by glucose; beta-cell tumor of the pancreas
No diabetes; access to insulin, as in a health care worker
**Known diabetes on insulin** with an extra dose, a missed meal or exercise
**Lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia and a large liver** since infancy

idea.rule: Hypoglycemia with high insulin and low C-peptide in a child means someone is injecting insulin.
also: Von Gierke disease adds lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia and a large liver

The physician must report suspected abuse

set_title: Vomiting, deep breathing or coma with ketones: diabetic ketoacidosis or a look-alike
stem: A 41-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 1 day of vomiting and abdominal pain. He drank heavily for 2 weeks and has eaten almost nothing for 4 days. He has no history of diabetes. Respirations are deep and rapid. Serum glucose is 82 mg/dL, arterial pH is 7.17, serum bicarbonate is 9 mEq/L, and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is markedly raised.
oneliner: 41M + 2 weeks of heavy drinking, little food for 4 days + vomiting and deep rapid breathing + glucose 82 + pH 7.17 + bicarbonate 9 + high beta-hydroxybutyrate → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Hyperosmolar state needs a glucose above 600 mg/dL and a normal pH; his glucose is **82 mg/dL** and his pH **7.17**
whyNot.B: Diabetic ketoacidosis requires hyperglycemia in a diabetic patient; he has **no diabetes** and a glucose of **82 mg/dL**
whyNot.C: Starvation ketosis is mild, with bicarbonate usually above 18 mEq/L; his bicarbonate is **9** with a pH of **7.17**
whyNot.D: Insulin excess lowers glucose and blocks ketones; he has **no diabetes** and a **bicarbonate of 9** with a raised beta-hydroxybutyrate

why: Heavy drinking with several days of starvation depletes glycogen, and ethanol metabolism raises the NADH to NAD+ ratio, which pushes acetoacetate toward beta-hydroxybutyrate. **Anion gap ketoacidosis with a normal or low glucose after a binge** is alcoholic ketoacidosis; treat with saline, dextrose and thiamine.

head: Glucose
pH and bicarbonate
Ketones
Serum osmolality
Typical patient and trigger
rows: Type 1 diabetes with missed insulin or an infection
pH above 7.30 and bicarbonate above 18 mEq/L
Older adult with type 2 diabetes, infection and poor fluid intake
Anion gap acidosis, often mixed with a vomiting alkalosis
Large beta-hydroxybutyrate; nitroprusside test may read weak
**Heavy drinking, then vomiting and days without food**
**Mild: bicarbonate usually above 18 mEq/L, pH near normal**
Insulin or sulfonylurea excess, with sweating and tremor

idea.rule: Ketoacidosis with a normal glucose after a binge = alcoholic ketoacidosis; with a very high glucose = DKA.
also: Vomiting adds a metabolic alkalosis, so the pH can be higher than the gap suggests
Dextrose stimulates insulin and clears the ketones
Give thiamine before or with glucose

set_title: Periods stopped, with or without milky discharge: pituitary, drug, thyroid, energy deficit or ovary
stem: A 29-year-old woman has had amenorrhea for 4 months and a milky discharge from both breasts; a pregnancy test is negative. She started risperidone 3 months ago. Her serum prolactin is 62 ng/mL and her TSH is normal.
oneliner: 29F + amenorrhea for 4 months + bilateral milky discharge + negative pregnancy test + risperidone started 3 months ago + prolactin 62 ng/mL + normal TSH → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: It follows postpartum hemorrhage and gives a **low prolactin** with failure to lactate; she has **galactorrhea** and a **high prolactin**
whyNot.C: A raised TRH can lift prolactin, but her **TSH is normal**
whyNot.D: It does not raise prolactin or cause **galactorrhea**; hers is **62 ng/mL** with a milky discharge
whyNot.E: An adenoma gives the same picture, but a **dopamine antagonist started 3 months ago** already explains the prolactin

why: Risperidone blocks D2 receptors on lactotrophs and removes the dopamine brake on prolactin. A **new dopamine antagonist** (risperidone, metoclopramide) explains the high prolactin, galactorrhea and amenorrhea, and stopping or switching the drug reverses it.

head: Prolactin
FSH and LH
TSH
Clincher
rows: No drug or thyroid cause; MRI shows a pituitary adenoma; treat with a dopamine agonist
**Dopamine antagonist** (risperidone, metoclopramide); prolactin falls when the drug stops
Raised TRH also stimulates lactotrophs; levothyroxine corrects the prolactin
Low weight and heavy training; low estradiol, low bone density, stress fractures
Postpartum hemorrhage with failure to lactate; low ACTH and cortisol cause orthostasis
Hot flashes and vaginal dryness; the ovary no longer makes estrogen or inhibin

idea.rule: High prolactin: no drug and normal TSH = tumor; dopamine antagonist = drug; high TSH = thyroid.
also: Metoclopramide also blocks D2 and raises prolactin
Aripiprazole, a partial agonist, is the antipsychotic least likely to do this
Check for pregnancy and TSH before blaming the drug

set_title: Confused or drowsy patient who drinks or has cirrhosis: the liver, thiamine, withdrawal or the kidneys
stem: A 45-year-old man is evaluated on the third day after an emergency appendectomy because he is agitated and says insects are crawling on the walls. He had been drinking heavily until the day of admission. Temperature is 38.4 C, pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 168/96 mm Hg. He is sweating and has a coarse tremor of the hands. Fingerstick glucose is 96 mg/dL.
oneliner: 45M + agitated, sees insects on day 3 after surgery + heavy drinking until admission + temperature 38.4 C + pulse 124 + BP 168/96 + sweating + tremor + glucose 96 → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Hepatic encephalopathy causes drowsiness and a flapping tremor in cirrhosis; he is **agitated** with **fever, tachycardia and hypertension**
whyNot.C: Wernicke encephalopathy gives nystagmus and ataxia without autonomic overactivity; he has **hallucinations, fever, pulse 124/min and sweating**
whyNot.D: Uremia needs kidney failure, which his history does not mention; he has **hallucinations, fever, sweating and hypertension** 3 days after his **last drink**
whyNot.A: Hypoglycemia needs a low glucose; his glucose is **96 mg/dL**

why: Chronic ethanol enhances GABA-A inhibition and blunts NMDA excitation; stopping it removes the inhibition and leaves unopposed excitatory and sympathetic drive. **Hallucinations with fever, tachycardia, hypertension and sweating about 3 days after the last drink** is delirium tremens, and benzodiazepines are first-line.

Neurologic signs
Deciding labs
Treatment
rows: Cirrhosis plus a trigger: GI bleeding, infection, constipation, sedatives or diuretics
Raised serum ammonia; stigmata of cirrhosis
Lactulose, which traps ammonium in the colon; rifaximin
Thiamine deficiency in a heavy drinker, at any time; a glucose load can precipitate it
**Confusion with nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia and a wide-based gait**
Low red cell transketolase activity; MRI may show mammillary body change
**2 to 4 days after the last drink**
Agitation, tremor and visual hallucinations with fever, tachycardia, hypertension and sweating
No specific test; check magnesium, potassium and glucose
Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam or chlordiazepoxide
Advanced kidney disease or missed dialysis
Confusion, asterixis, itching, pericardial friction rub
**Markedly raised urea nitrogen and creatinine with metabolic acidosis**

idea.rule: Hallucinations + autonomic storm 2 to 4 days after the last drink = delirium tremens.
also: Withdrawal seizures peak earlier, at 12 to 48 hours
Mortality falls with early benzodiazepine treatment
Replace thiamine and magnesium

set_title: Spells of staring, jerking or an odd smell: which kind of seizure, or not a seizure
stem: A 45-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department following a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. He drinks several beers and spirits every day, and his last drink was about 30 hours ago. His pulse is 118/min and his hands tremble.
oneliner: 45M + single generalized seizure + daily heavy drinking, last drink 30 hours ago + tremor and tachycardia → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Convulsive syncope from a vasovagal faint

whyNot.B: A focal impaired awareness seizure shows automatisms and focal onset; his was **generalized, 30 hours after his last drink**
whyNot.C: A seizure with intact awareness does not cause loss of consciousness; his seizure was **generalized tonic-clonic**
whyNot.D: Absence seizures are brief staring spells in children; he is **45 and had a tonic-clonic seizure**
whyNot.E: Convulsive syncope causes seconds of jerking with prompt recovery; his seizure was **generalized tonic-clonic with tremor and a fast pulse** after stopping alcohol

why: Long-term alcohol use up-regulates NMDA receptors and down-regulates GABA-A receptors, so stopping leaves the brain hyperexcitable. **A generalized seizure with tremor and tachycardia about 1 day after the last drink** is alcohol withdrawal; a benzodiazepine treats it.

Length
Awareness and automatisms
After the spell and EEG
rows: Any age; temporal lobe focus is the most common
**Awareness lost, with lip smacking or hand picking (automatisms)**
Confused for minutes; focal temporal spikes
**Awareness kept**; aura such as a foul smell, or jerking that marches up a limb
Back to normal at once; focal spikes may appear
Under 30 seconds, many times a day
Stares with eyelid flutter; no aura
No confusion afterward; **3-Hz spike-and-wave**; hyperventilation provokes it
**Generalized tonic-clonic seizure 6 to 48 hours after the last drink**
Awareness lost; tremor, sweating and a fast pulse
Postictal state; EEG usually normal; benzodiazepine treats it
Any age; triggered by standing, a blood draw or a cough
Jerking lasts only seconds after pallor
**Alert within a minute; no tongue biting or confusion**; EEG normal

idea.rule: Heavy daily drinker + generalized seizure 6 to 48 hours after the last drink + tremor and tachycardia = withdrawal seizure.
also: Seizures occur 6 to 48 hours after the last drink; delirium tremens follows at 48 to 96 hours
Benzodiazepines are first line
Phenytoin does not prevent withdrawal seizures

set_title: The drinker who gets sick: withdrawal, low glucose, a drug interaction or a damaged liver
stem: A 58-year-old woman who drinks a bottle of wine daily is hospitalized for a hip replacement. On day 2 she is tremulous, diaphoretic, and sees insects crawling on the wall. Pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 164/98 mm Hg.
oneliner: 58F + daily wine + hospitalized for hip replacement + day 2 tremor, sweating, visual hallucinations + pulse 118/min → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Acetaminophen toxicity presents with right upper quadrant pain and raised transaminases; **she has tremor, hallucinations and high blood pressure**
whyNot.B: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome gives confusion, ataxia and eye signs; **she has hallucinations with sweating, pulse 118/min and BP 164/98 mm Hg**
whyNot.D: A disulfiram-like reaction follows drinking while on a drug such as metronidazole; **she has been in hospital and has hallucinations**
whyNot.E: Alcoholic hypoglycemia occurs during a binge and causes coma; **she has been in hospital for 2 days with hypertension and hallucinations**

why: Chronic ethanol enhances GABA-A inhibition and blocks NMDA receptors. When intake stops, inhibition falls and glutamate excites unopposed. **Tremor, sweating, hypertension and hallucinations 2 days after drinking stops** is alcohol withdrawal.

Main signs
Key lab
Mechanism
rows: **6 to 72 hours after the last drink; delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours**
Tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, hallucinations, seizures

During or just after a binge with no food

High NADH to NAD+ ratio shunts pyruvate to lactate and blocks gluconeogenesis

also: Benzodiazepines are first-line; long-acting agents are preferred
Seizures peak at 12 to 48 hours; delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours
Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia are common

set_title: Abnormal movements after an antipsychotic: which reaction and when
stem: A 24-year-old woman is given intramuscular haloperidol in the emergency department for severe agitation. Three hours later her jaw is clenched and her neck is turned sharply to the right. Her temperature is 37.1°C.
oneliner: 24F + intramuscular haloperidol 3 hours ago + clenched jaw, neck turned sharply to one side, temperature 37.1°C → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needs high fever and rigidity with a raised creatine kinase; her **temperature is 37.1°C** and the problem began **3 hours** after an injection
whyNot.C: Tardive dyskinesia follows months to years of treatment; she has **3 hours of treatment with a fixed neck and jaw posture**
whyNot.D: Parkinson disease evolves over years; her **sustained neck and jaw spasm began 3 hours after an injection**
whyNot.E: Drug-induced parkinsonism gives slowness and rigidity over days to weeks; she has **a sudden fixed posture of the neck and jaw within hours**

why: Acute dystonia is a sustained muscle spasm within hours to days of a dopamine blocker, and it is most common with high-potency drugs in young patients. **A fixed neck and jaw posture hours after an injection, with a normal temperature,** is an acute dystonic reaction. Benztropine or diphenhydramine relieves it.

head: Timing after the drug
Movement or tone
Fever and creatine kinase
Treatment
rows: Hours to days after starting or raising a dose
**Sustained spasm of neck, jaw or eye muscles (torticollis, oculogyric crisis)**
Lower the dose or switch drug; benztropine
Days to weeks, often after a dose rise
Marked lead-pipe rigidity with confusion and unstable blood pressure
**High fever with creatine kinase far above normal**
Stop the drug; dantrolene or bromocriptine; cooling
**Lip smacking, tongue protrusion and writhing of the fingers**
Switch to clozapine or add a VMAT2 inhibitor; anticholinergics worsen it
No link to a drug; gradual over years
**One-sided resting tremor that spreads, with slowness and rigidity**

idea.rule: Sudden fixed spasm of the neck, jaw or eyes within hours of a dopamine blocker = acute dystonia.
also: Oculogyric crisis and torticollis are typical
Young men on high-potency drugs are most at risk

set_title: Abnormal movements after an antipsychotic: which reaction and when
stem: A 63-year-old man has taken haloperidol for 11 years. He has repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and writhing movements of the fingers. His temperature is 36.9°C and muscle tone is normal.
oneliner: 63M + haloperidol for 11 years + lip smacking, tongue protrusion, finger writhing, normal tone and temperature → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Drug-induced parkinsonism gives symmetric slowness and rigidity within weeks; he has **involuntary writhing movements with normal tone after 11 years**
whyNot.B: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome gives fever and rigidity; his **temperature is 36.9°C and tone is normal**
whyNot.C: Acute dystonia appears within hours to days of a dose; he has **11 years of treatment with repetitive orofacial movements**
whyNot.E: Parkinson disease gives slowness, rigidity and a resting tremor; he has **normal tone with lip smacking and finger writhing**

why: Long-term dopamine receptor blockade is thought to make postsynaptic receptors supersensitive. **Lip smacking, tongue protrusion and writhing fingers after years of an antipsychotic** is tardive dyskinesia. Anticholinergics worsen it, and a VMAT2 inhibitor or a switch to clozapine helps.

set_title: New mother who is anxious, tearful or not herself: blues, depression, psychosis, OCD or the thyroid

whyNot.D: Postpartum thyroiditis causes palpitations and weight loss; she has **contamination fears with wiping rituals and a normal mood**
whyNot.E: Postpartum depression needs low mood or loss of pleasure; her **mood, sleep and appetite are normal**

why: Obsessions and compulsions that the patient recognizes as excessive are ego-dystonic. **Unwanted contamination fears with rituals and intact insight and normal mood** are obsessive-compulsive disorder; an SSRI such as sertraline and cognitive behavioral therapy are used.

whyNot.C: Postpartum depression needs symptoms lasting at least 2 weeks; she is **3 days after delivery**
whyNot.D: Obsessive-compulsive disorder involves intrusive thoughts and rituals; she **reports no intrusive thoughts**
